## Abstract:

This paper presents an AI-powered framework that automates the generation of Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for chemistry laboratories. The proposed solution integrates Generative AI, large language models (LLMs), and a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture enhanced with a Chroma database and prompt engineering techniques. Together, these components enable the creation of accurate, customizable, and context-aware SOPs tailored to specific laboratory equipment, materials, and processes. SOPs play a vital role in ensuring safety, consistency, and regulatory compliance in chemical operations. Our system allows users to select and customize sections, such as safety guidelines, calibration steps, or procedural details, while automatically retrieving verified information from trusted sources, including equipment manuals and scientific literature. This approach minimizes hallucinations and ensures factual precision, which is crucial in chemistry workflows. By combining LLMs with semantic retrieval, the framework significantly reduces the time and effort required for SOP preparation while maintaining high standards of accuracy and safety. The results highlight how GenAI can transform laboratory documentation, offering a scalable solution for research and industrial chemical applications.

SECTION I.

## Introduction

In chemistry, SOPs serve as the foundation for maintaining experimental consistency, laboratory safety, and regulatory compliance. Chemists rely on well defined SOPs to standardize procedures, ensuring reproducibility in research and industrial applications. Precise documentation of chemical handling, synthesis methods, and analytical techniques is essential not only for accuracy but also for adherence to safety protocols, particularly when working with hazardous substances. Regulatory bodies such as the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) mandate strict adherence to SOPs to mitigate risks associated with chemical exposure, waste disposal, and process safety [1]. However, traditional SOP documentation remains a labor intensive and error prone process, often requiring significant manual effort to align with evolving regulatory frameworks and advancements in chemical methodologies. This challenge highlights the necessity for an automated, intelligent system capable of dynamically generating and optimizing SOPs to support chemists in maintaining high standards of laboratory operation.

Existing SOP management approaches typically rely on static document repositories or manual templates that focus primarily on storage and retrieval rather than intelligent generation or contextual adaptation. While such frameworks ensure document availability, they lack the ability to dynamically generate SOPs tailored to specific laboratory equipment, materials, and operational constraints. More recently, generic AI-based text generation tools have been explored for documentation tasks; however, when applied to safety-critical domains such as chemistry, these models suffer from key limitations, including factual hallucinations, insufficient domain grounding, and limited traceability to authoritative sources. These shortcomings pose significant risks in laboratory environments, where inaccurate procedures may compromise safety or regulatory compliance.

The integration of AI-powered language models into SOP generation presents a transformative approach to addressing these challenges. By leveraging retrieval augmented generation (RAG) and Chroma databases, AI driven SOPs can dynamically pull information from established chemical literature, equipment manuals, and safety guidelines, ensuring that generated procedures remain scientifically sound and up-to-date. This capability is particularly valuable in fields such as analytical chemistry, where methods must adhere to Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) guidelines, or in synthetic chemistry, where reaction conditions must be meticulously documented to ensure reproducibility and safety [2]. Furthermore, AI driven SOP optimization allows chemists to customize procedural elements, incorporating real time hazard assessments and regulatory updates, thereby reducing the risk of non compliance and enhancing overall laboratory efficiency. Unlike generic generative frameworks, the proposed architecture constrains the generation process using semantically retrieved domain-specific knowledge, significantly reducing hallucination risks and improving procedural reliability. The proposed framework further enables modular and customizable SOP generation, allowing users to select or refine sections such as safety guidelines, calibration steps, or waste disposal protocols, while ensuring traceability to verified reference documents. By automating SOP creation while preserving the accuracy and reliability demanded in the chemical sciences, this approach establishes a new paradigm for laboratory documentation, bridging the gap between traditional chemical methodologies and modern AI advancements.

The loss of an SOP in a laboratory setting can lead to significant disruptions, impacting research continuity, safety, and compliance. Common scenarios where SOPs may be misplaced include accidental deletion from digital records, damage to physical copies due to chemical spills, or personnel turnover where critical procedural knowledge is not effectively transferred. In regulated environments such as pharmaceutical and analytical chemistry laboratories, the absence of an SOP can halt experimental workflows, delay production, and even lead to regulatory violations [3].

SECTION II.

## State of Art

Although large language models and retrieval-augmented generation techniques have demonstrated strong performance in general natural language processing tasks, their use in chemistry remains relatively limited and task specific. Current research primarily applies LLMs to molecular design [5], reaction prediction [6], and chemical text analysis [7], while the automated generation of laboratory Standard Operating Procedures has not been systematically addressed. To the best of our knowledge, no existing LLM-RAG framework has been proposed or experimentally evaluated for chemistry specific SOP automation, particularly in safety critical and regulation driven laboratory settings.

### A. Standard Operating Procedures in Chemistry

Standard Operating Procedures play a fundamental role in ensuring experimental reproducibility, regulatory compliance, and safety in chemical research and industrial applications. The development of SOPs has evolved from informal practices in early research laboratories to formalized frameworks embedded within Good Laboratory Practices (GLP) and regulatory standards since the mid-20th century [8]. This evolution reflects growing societal and regulatory demands for safety, reproducibility, and accountability in chemical handling and experimentation [9]. Properly structured SOPs help in minimizing variability in chemical processes, ensuring adherence to international guidelines such as ISO 9001 and Good Laboratory Practices (GLP), and reducing hazards associated with handling chemicals and equipment [10]. Hence, the significance of SOPs is underscored by statistics indicating persistent laboratory accidents linked to procedural deficiencies, emphasizing the need for robust procedural frameworks [11]. However, manual SOP creation is often time consuming, prone to inconsistencies, and difficult to maintain as procedures evolve with new scientific discoveries and technological advancements [12].

These limitations are further exacerbated in many laboratory settings where outdated SOPs can lead to misuse of chemicals, improper equipment calibration, and non compliance with safety standards [13]. Moreover, lost or inaccessible SOPs disrupt laboratory workflows, delay critical experiments, and increase the risk of accidents [14]. Together, these challenges highlight the urgent need for automated and dynamic SOP management systems capable of adapting to evolving laboratory needs.

### B. AI-Driven Documentation and Automated SOP Generation

Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly in Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Generative AI (GenAI), have paved the way for automating complex documentation tasks, including SOP generation. Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT-4, BERT, and T5 have demonstrated the ability to generate technical and regulatory documents with high accuracy and contextual relevance [15], [16]. Many models, such as RoBERTa and GPT-2, have been fine tuned to automate software documentation, significantly improving accuracy and reducing training losses. RoBERTa, in particular, has demonstrated superior performance with an accuracy score of 99.94% compared to GPT-2’s 74.37% [17].

Despite these advancements, one of the primary concerns in using AI generated documentation in scientific fields is the risk of hallucinations, where AI models produce factually incorrect or misleading information [18]. In addition to factual reliability, there are challenges related to security and privacy, where systems must comply with data protection regulations and maintain patient confidentiality [19]. Furthermore, AI systems can inadvertently perpetuate or even exacerbate existing biases present in the data they are trained on [20], raising ethical considerations for their deployment in high stakes domains.

Because chemistry-specific automated SOP generation has limited direct benchmarked prior work, the most relevant and best performing methodological family for comparison is retrieval grounded generation, where LLM outputs are constrained using semantically retrieved authoritative documents [7], [21], [22]. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) was introduced to improve factuality in knowledge intensive generation tasks by combining retrieval with generation. Subsequent surveys and high impact studies consistently report that retrieval grounded pipelines outperform retrieval free generative approaches in terms of factual accuracy, credibility, and robustness, particularly for technical and scientific content [23], [24], [25]. Furthermore, advances in dense retrieval models have demonstrated strong performance in retrieving relevant passages for downstream generation tasks, improving end-to-end system reliability in knowledge intensive applications [26], [27], [28].

To address these limitations and enhance the reliability and domain specific accuracy of AI-generated SOPs, the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework has emerged as a powerful approach [29]. By integrating a Chroma database, AI models can retrieve validated scientific literature, regulatory documents, and equipment manuals, ensuring that SOPs are generated based on authentic and up-to-date sources. This hybrid approach not only improves content precision but also enables customizable SOP generation, allowing users to specify required sections such as safety protocols, calibration procedures, waste disposal guidelines, and experimental steps [30]. However, most existing RAG-based systems focus on general NLP tasks such as question answering [31], summarization [32], or open-domain text generation [33]. Experimental validation in highly regulated, domain-specific documentation tasks such as chemistry SOP generation remains largely unexplored in the literature.

### C. The Need for AI-Powered SOP Solutions in Chemistry

Despite the advancements in AI-driven text generation, domain specific SOP automation in chemistry remains an underexplored area. Existing document management systems primarily focus on SOP storage and retrieval rather than automated generation [34]. Some AI assisted documentation tools are available in the healthcare and pharmaceutical industries [35], but they lack the flexibility required for chemistry specific workflows, where experimental conditions, materials, and safety measures vary significantly.

From a comparative and experimental perspective, the closest available baselines for chemistry SOP generation are: (i) retrieval-free LLM-based generation using prompt-only approaches, and (ii) retrieval grounded generation pipelines that constrain outputs using authoritative reference documents. Recent research has emphasized the importance of evaluating such systems using quantitative and modular evaluation strategies that separately assess retrieval quality and generation faithfulness. Reference free and similarity based evaluation frameworks have been proposed to enable progressive comparison between retrieval free and retrieval grounded systems under controlled conditions, particularly in scenarios where ground-truth documents exist but are intentionally withheld. In contrast to existing work, this study introduces an AI-powered SOP generation framework specifically tailored to chemical laboratory environments and experimentally validates its effectiveness through controlled SOP reconstruction experiments, similarity based evaluation metrics, and benchmark scenarios across multiple analytical instruments. By aligning the experimental design with emerging best practices for evaluating retrieval-augmented generation systems, this work provides measurable evidence of novelty, reliability, and progressive improvement over retrieval-free generative baselines.

### A. Data Collection

One of the most challenging aspects of this work was gathering data for Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) from a variety of sources. SOPs, often referred to as the blueprint or instruction manual for how tasks are executed in an organization, are critical documents that outline step-by-step processes to ensure consistency, efficiency, and compliance. They serve as a reference for employees, contractors, and stakeholders to follow established procedures accurately. However, despite their importance, collecting high quality and diverse SOP data is notoriously difficult due to issues such as access restrictions, variability in formats, and the ever changing nature of operational requirements.

In this work, the SOP dataset was constructed using multiple complementary sources to build a comprehensive and representative database suitable for automated SOP generation. The final dataset consists of a total of 108 documents, including 96 SOP documents, and 12 equipment manuals. SOPs were collected primarily from publicly available online repositories, academic and industrial laboratory documentation, and direct contributions from colleagues and industry professionals actively involved in laboratory operations. These contributions enabled the inclusion of real-world SOPs currently in use across different organizational settings. [Table 1](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/) summarizes the analytical equipment, manufacturers, material types, and laboratory contexts represented in the SOP and equipment manual dataset.

Recognizing the limitations of relying solely on traditional SOP documents, this work also incorporated equipment manuals as a supplemental data source. Equipment manuals, which are widely available and often more detailed, provide step-by-step instructions for operating and maintaining specific devices. These manuals not only align closely with the structure and intent of SOPs but also offer technical depth and accuracy. By including these manuals alongside SOPs, the database was enriched with reliable, contextually relevant information, addressing one of the critical flaws in traditional SOP systems: the risk of hallucination. In the context of Generative AI, hallucination refers to the generation of plausible sounding but factually incorrect or unsupported content. The inclusion of equipment manuals mitigates this risk by providing a robust factual grounding for the model during the retrieval and generation phases.

Moreover, the integration of equipment manuals allowed for the enhancement and expansion of the database, filling gaps where SOPs were unavailable or difficult to obtain. Manuals are typically written by experts with a deep understanding of the equipment and processes involved, ensuring high quality data. Their standardized format and detailed descriptions make them an ideal supplement for SOP data, especially for use cases requiring high levels of technical accuracy and specificity.

### B. Content Division and Model Integration Into LangChain

The process begins with gathering and loading all relevant documents required for building the SOP generation system. This step is executed using the load_documents function, which utilizes the PyPDFDirectoryLoader from LangChain. LangChain is a powerful framework designed to assist in creating applications that leverage large language models (LLMs) [36]. It simplifies the integration of various data sources, processing pipelines, and retrieval mechanisms into a unified workflow. Specifically, LangChain’s PyPDFDirectoryLoader is used to scan a specified directory (DATA_PATH) and extract the content of all PDF files contained within it.

The extracted content is then converted into Document objects, a standardized format provided by LangChain that includes metadata such as file names and page numbers along with the text content. This standardization ensures consistent handling of diverse file formats and structures, which is essential for downstream processing. Moreover, LangChain’s modular design allows seamless integration with other components, such as text splitters, vector databases, and LLMs, making it an ideal choice for complex workflows like SOP generation. By leveraging LangChain’s capabilities in this step, the system efficiently builds a robust dataset that serves as the foundation for the SOP generation pipeline. This framework not only streamlines the loading process but also provides a scalable solution for managing large volumes of heterogeneous documents, ensuring that the data is well organized and ready for subsequent operations such as chunking, embedding, and semantic retrieval. This step is vital for creating a seamless pipeline where data can flow consistently and accurately across all stages of the process.

### C. Embedding Documents Into a Vector Space

Once the SOP documents are divided into manageable chunks, the next step involves embedding these chunks into a high dimensional vector space. This is achieved using OpenAI’s advanced embedding functions, which transform the textual data into numerical vectors. These vectors are designed to capture the semantic meaning of the content, allowing for an in depth understanding of the relationships between different chunks. In this implementation, document chunks were embedded using OpenAI’s embedding function with an explicitly specified embedding model **text-embedding-3-small**. Prior to embedding, documents were segmented using a RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter configured with a chunk size of **800 characters** and an overlap of **80 characters**. This configuration was selected to preserve sufficient procedural continuity (e.g., multi-step calibration and safety sequences) while maintaining retrieval granularity, thereby reducing the risk that unrelated SOP sections are embedded into the same chunk. The overlap ensures that boundary information (e.g., warnings, prerequisites, or step transitions) is not lost during splitting and remains retrievable.

The embedding process is a critical component of the system, as it provides the foundation for semantic retrieval. By representing text as vectors in a high dimensional space, the system enables efficient comparison and ranking of chunks based on their relevance to user queries. This transformation not only preserves the contextual meaning of the original text but also enhances the system’s ability to retrieve information accurately and quickly.

### D. Vector Store Integration with Chroma

After embedding the document chunks into a high-dimensional vector space, the next step involves storing and managing these embeddings in Chroma, a high performance vector database [37]. Chroma plays a pivotal role in the system by enabling efficient semantic retrieval of relevant information. Using the add_to_chroma function, the embeddings are stored in a structured and searchable format, alongside their metadata, which includes file names, page numbers, and contextual tags. This metadata ensures that each retrieved chunk remains traceable to its original source, enhancing the reliability and transparency of the system.

When a user query is issued, it is first transformed into an embedding using the same OpenAI embedding function employed during the document embedding phase. This ensures that both the query and the stored embeddings exist within the same semantic space. Chroma then performs similarity searches, comparing the query embedding to the stored vectors using metrics such as cosine similarity. The results are ranked based on relevance, ensuring that the most pertinent chunks are retrieved and passed to the subsequent generation phase.

Chroma’s capabilities extend beyond retrieval efficiency. Its scalable architecture allows it to handle large volumes of data, making it suitable for managing the growing complexity of SOP databases. Furthermore, Chroma supports dynamic updates, enabling new embeddings to be added or outdated ones to be removed seamlessly. This adaptability ensures that the system remains current and responsive to evolving datasets while generating SOP.

### E. Building the RAG System

The Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) framework forms the backbone of the SOP generation system, seamlessly combining semantic retrieval and generative capabilities. After the document chunks are embedded and stored in the Chroma vector database, the RAG system uses semantic similarity metrics to identify and retrieve the most contextually relevant chunks based on user queries. These chunks are then augmented with supplemental information extracted from equipment manuals and other trusted sources to ensure the input to the generative model is comprehensive and reliable. The RAG system relies on OpenAI’s API to power its language model, leveraging its advanced generative capabilities to transform the retrieved and augmented information into detailed SOP sections. By dynamically integrating retrieval and generation, the RAG system ensures that the generated SOPs are accurate, user focused, and tailored to the specific needs of chemical laboratory workflows.

### F. Prompt Engineering

Prompt engineering is a pivotal step in the SOP generation pipeline, as it enables the large language model (LLM) to transform retrieved content into coherent, contextually accurate, and highly detailed SOP sections. Following semantic retrieval from the Chroma vector database, carefully designed prompts guide the LLM to structure its output according to predefined SOP requirements. These prompts are explicitly tailored to the chemical domain and organized into standardized sections such as Scope, Background, Safety, Calibration, and Quality Control, ensuring comprehensive coverage of critical laboratory workflows.

The structure and content of the RAG prompt template are grounded in established regulatory and industry standard SOP frameworks. In particular, the inclusion of sections such as Scope, Safety, Materials and Equipment, Procedure, Calibration, and Quality Control is informed by Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) guidelines, Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) laboratory safety standards, and widely adopted SOP formats used in academic, industrial, and pharmaceutical laboratories. By embedding these regulatory aligned structural constraints directly into the prompt, the template ensures that generated SOPs meet compliance requirements while guiding the LLM to produce detailed, operational, and safety-conscious procedural instructions rather than high-level summaries.

Each prompt is meticulously designed to include contextual instructions derived from the retrieved chunks and any additional information extracted from equipment manuals. For example, when generating a calibration section, the prompt specifies exact procedural details, avoiding vague instructions like “refer to the manufacturer’s manual.” Instead, it requests step-by-step actions, including specific buttons to press on the instrument interface, ensuring the generated SOP is both actionable and domain specific. This grounding in factual data significantly reduces the risk of hallucinations, a common issue in generative AI, by ensuring the model’s output remains firmly tied to the retrieved context.

The prompts are not static; they are dynamically structured to provide flexibility for customization. Users can specify whether to include or exclude certain sections, such as waste disposal protocols or safety guidelines, tailoring the generated SOP to their specific requirements. Additionally, the prompts are optimized to enforce consistency and clarity, ensuring the outputs maintain a professional tone while aligning with regulatory standards. This is particularly crucial in the chemical industry, where precise instructions and compliance are non negotiable.

To enhance usability, the prompts adopt a modular and iterative approach. Each SOP section is generated independently, allowing for seamless integration into the final document. Prompts are designed to elicit responses that include technical depth, examples, and practical applications, ensuring that even complex procedures are explained in an accessible and step-by-step manner. For instance, safety sections may detail specific risks associated with chemicals and equipment, supplemented by clear instructions for handling hazardous materials.

To operationalize this framework, a structured Retrieval Augmented Generation prompt template was implemented, as shown in [Table 3](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/). This template encapsulates the entire instruction logic used to generate each SOP section, covering all ten predefined categories—from Scope and Background to Limitations and Documentation. It allows the dynamic insertion of context retrieved from the Chroma vector store through variables such as context and section, and serves as the bridge between retrieval and generation, ensuring that every SOP produced by the system adheres to laboratory standards, procedural reproducibility, and quality assurance benchmarks.

SECTION IV.

## Validation and Quality Control

To validate the reliability and accuracy of our SOP generation system, a controlled scenario was designed and executed. This scenario involved an existing SOP, for which all details and information were fully known and documented. The SOP was then deliberately hidden from the system, and all references, data, and related information about it were removed from the database and document repository. This ensured that the system had no direct knowledge or prior exposure to the target SOP. The objective was to evaluate whether the system, following the steps outlined in the methodology, could regenerate a comparable SOP purely through its retrieval, augmentation, and generation pipeline.

After removing the SOP, the program was run through all steps of the methodology. It loaded and split documents, generated embeddings, stored them in Chroma for semantic retrieval, and constructed the SOP using the RAG framework and prompt engineering. The generated SOP was then compared to the original hidden SOP to evaluate how accurately the system recreated the document. This comparison was achieved using a similarity calculation function based on TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) vectorization and cosine similarity, implemented as follows:

1.   Extracting Text Content: The text content of both the original SOP and the system-generated SOP was extracted. Depending on the file format (either.docx or.pdf), specific extraction methods were applied to ensure consistent text representation.

2.   Text Vectorization: TF-IDF vectorization was applied to transform the textual data into numerical vectors. This technique assigns weights to terms in the document, with higher weights given to terms that are more important (i.e., terms that appear frequently in one document but rarely across others). This representation captures the unique characteristics of each document.

3.   Cosine Similarity Calculation: Once the documents were vectorized, cosine similarity was used to measure the degree of similarity between the two vector representations. Cosine similarity calculates the cosine of the angle between two vectors in a high-dimensional space, with values ranging from -1 to 1:

    *   A value of 1 indicates perfect similarity (identical vectors).

    *   A value of 0 indicates no similarity (orthogonal vectors).

    *   A value of -1 indicates complete dissimilarity.

 For this system, cosine similarity focused on positive correlations, meaning that higher values (closer to 1) indicated greater similarity between the original and generated SOPs.
4.   Validation Results: The similarity scores for different SOPs across various materials and procedures consistently ranged between 0.8 and 0.9 in this work, demonstrating a high degree of alignment between the generated and original SOPs. This range indicates that the system effectively reconstructed the critical content, structure, and procedural details of the original SOPs, despite having no direct information about them.

To further assess performance consistency across different instruments and experimental setups, three benchmark scenarios were designed and evaluated, as summarized in [Table 4](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/). Each scenario corresponded to a distinct analytical instrument: Gas Chromatography–Mass Spectrometry (GC/MS) (Scenario 1), Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) (Scenario 2), and Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICPMS) (Scenario 3). Scenarios 1 and 2 included the availability of manuals (manufacturer documentation), whereas Scenario 3 lacked such references, providing a useful contrast for evaluating the system’s reliance on external guidance during SOP generation.

[![Image 6: Table 4- Benchmark Scenarios for SOP Generation Accuracy](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/mediastore/IEEE/content/media/6287639/11323511/11370815/mallo.t4-3660770-small.gif)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/mediastore/IEEE/content/media/6287639/11323511/11370815/mallo.t4-3660770-large.gif)

The similarity between the generated and reference SOPs, measured through cosine similarity, yielded accuracy values of **0.84** for GC/MS, **0.75** for FTIR, and **0.83** for ICPMS. Higher similarity scores were consistently obtained in cases where the original manuals or detailed documentation were available, underscoring the critical role of structured reference data in improving retrieval quality and semantic precision. In contrast, when such documentation was absent, the generated SOPs exhibited slightly reduced contextual precision and completeness, suggesting that the model relied more heavily on general knowledge embeddings rather than specific procedural context. These findings highlight that while the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework demonstrates strong autonomous reasoning and content reconstruction capabilities, the availability of rich contextual data substantially enhances its performance. Overall, the benchmark results confirm that the system achieves high reliability and reproducibility across diverse laboratory instruments, with all similarity scores within the high-confidence range (higher than 0.75). This validates the robustness and practical applicability of the proposed methodology for automated SOP reconstruction and laboratory quality assurance.

In addition to quantitative similarity based validation, all generated SOP documents were also subjected to qualitative expert review. A chemistry domain expert with laboratory experience manually examined the generated SOPs to assess their scientific correctness, procedural completeness, regulatory compliance, and practical operability. The expert evaluation focused on verifying the accuracy of safety instructions, calibration steps, material handling procedures, and overall logical consistency of the SOPs. This qualitative assessment confirmed that the generated SOPs were technically sound, aligned with standard laboratory practices, and suitable for real-world chemical laboratory use. The combined use of quantitative similarity metrics and expert-driven qualitative evaluation provides a more comprehensive validation of the proposed system’s reliability and practical applicability.

SECTION V.

## Risk Mitigation, Human-in-the-Loop Validation, and Deployment Safeguards

Despite the advantages of AI-powered SOP generation, the deployment of such systems in safety critical laboratory environments requires careful consideration of potential risks, ethical implications, and operational safeguards. This work explicitly acknowledges that AI-generated SOPs, if used without oversight, may introduce failure modes that could compromise laboratory safety or regulatory compliance.

### A. Failure Mode Analysis

Potential failure modes associated with automated SOP generation include, but are not limited to:

*   omission or incorrect sequencing of calibration steps for analytical instruments,

*   incomplete specification of personal protective equipment (PPE) requirements,

*   insufficient hazard identification for chemicals or materials involved, and

*   ambiguity in waste disposal or emergency response procedures.

To mitigate these risks, the proposed framework relies on retrieval grounded generation, ensuring that all procedural content is anchored to authoritative reference documents such as validated SOPs, equipment manuals, and regulatory guidelines. This grounding significantly reduces the likelihood of unsafe procedural hallucinations compared to retrieval-free generative approaches.

### B. Human-in-the-Loop Validation

The system is explicitly designed to operate under a human-in-the-loop paradigm. All generated SOPs are intended to be reviewed, validated, and approved by qualified laboratory personnel (e.g., chemists, safety officers, or quality managers) prior to operational use. As documented in the validation process, domain experts manually verified generated SOPs for factual correctness, safety compliance, procedural completeness, and practical operability. This human validation layer acts as a critical safeguard, ensuring that AI-generated outputs support, rather than replace, professional judgment.

### C. Legal and Ethical Considerations

From a legal and ethical perspective, the system is positioned as a decision support and documentation assistance tool, not an autonomous authority for laboratory operations. Final responsibility for SOP approval, enforcement, and compliance remains with the laboratory management and designated safety personnel. This distinction is essential to align with regulatory frameworks such as GLP, OSHA, and CGMP, which mandate human accountability for procedural compliance and risk management. Furthermore, the framework promotes transparency and traceability by maintaining metadata links between generated SOP sections and their source documents. This traceability supports auditability, regulatory inspections, and accountability key ethical requirements in regulated laboratory environments.

### D. Deployment Safeguards

To ensure safe deployment, the proposed system incorporates several safeguards:

*   Mandatory expert review before SOP finalization

*   Traceable retrieval of source documents for every generated section

*   Modular SOP generation to prevent uncontrolled content propagation

*   Explicit disclaimers indicating advisory usage

*   Support for periodic updates as regulations or equipment specifications evolve

These safeguards collectively ensure that the system enhances efficiency and consistency while maintaining strict adherence to safety, ethical responsibility, and regulatory compliance.

SECTION VI.

## User Interface for Enhanced SOP Generation

The Enhanced SOP Generator interface shown in [Figure 3](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/) is a user-friendly tool designed to facilitate the creation of detailed and professional SOPs without requiring programming expertise. Built using the Python Tkinter library, the GUI provides a seamless experience for users, allowing them to generate customized SOPs for various instruments and procedures.

[![Image 7: FIGURE 3. - Graphical user interface of the enhanced SOP generator.](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/mediastore/IEEE/content/media/6287639/11323511/11370815/mallo3-3660770-small.gif)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/mediastore/IEEE/content/media/6287639/11323511/11370815/mallo3-3660770-large.gif)

Graphical user interface of the enhanced SOP generator.

[![Image 8: FIGURE 4. - Workflow of the SOP generation process.](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/mediastore/IEEE/content/media/6287639/11323511/11370815/mallo4-3660770-small.gif)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/mediastore/IEEE/content/media/6287639/11323511/11370815/mallo4-3660770-large.gif)

**FIGURE 4.**

Workflow of the SOP generation process.

The interface includes the following key components:

*   Instrument-Specific Inputs: Users can specify the instrument’s name, brand, and model. These details ensure that the generated SOP is tailored to the equipment being used, enhancing its relevance and accuracy.

*   Manual Upload Feature: Users can upload optional manuals in PDF format, which are processed and integrated into the SOP generation pipeline. This feature enriches the contextual database, ensuring the SOPs include highly relevant and detailed content from external references.

*   Material Type Selection: A dropdown menu allows users to select the material type (e.g., liquid or solid). This input is incorporated into the SOP to refine procedural details and ensure compatibility with the specified material properties.

*   Section Selection: Users can select which sections of the SOP to include, such as “Scope,” “Safety,” “Materials and Equipment,” “Calibration,” and “Procedure.” A “Select All” option is also available for comprehensive SOP generation. The modularity ensures flexibility in creating SOPs specific to the user’s needs.

*   Output Path Specification: Users can choose where to save the final SOP document in Word format. This functionality ensures that the output is easy to access and share.

*   Professional Customization: The system supports the inclusion of a company logo, adding a professional touch to the generated SOPs. The logo is dynamically included in the Word document header, enhancing branding.

*   Integration with Advanced AI Models: The backend utilizes LangChain for document loading and splitting, Chroma for semantic search and retrieval, and OpenAI models for SOP content generation. These technologies ensure the generated SOPs are precise, contextually relevant, and adhere to professional standards.

*   Error Handling and Guidance: The interface includes validation for required fields and provides clear error messages if essential information is missing. This feature makes the tool accessible even for non-technical users.

The overall workflow of the system is summarized in [Figure 3](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/), which illustrates how user inputs, similarity search, and AI-driven content generation are integrated. Hence, the SOP Generator empowers users to streamline the creation of SOPs, saving time and ensuring compliance with industry standards. With its intuitive design, dynamic features, and robust AI-driven backend, this tool bridges the gap between technical documentation requirements and practical usability.

SECTION VII.

## Conclusion and Future Work

In conclusion, this work presents a comprehensive and innovative approach to automating Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) generation using advanced AI frameworks. By integrating data collection from diverse sources, semantic embedding, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) techniques, the proposed system is capable of producing accurate and contextually relevant SOPs tailored to the rigorous demands of chemical laboratory workflows. The system leverages state-of-the-art tools such as LangChain for document processing, OpenAI’s embedding functions for semantic representation, and the Chroma vector database for efficient retrieval, thereby ensuring that generated SOPs are both reliable and up-to-date. The incorporation of equipment manuals as supplementary data sources further enriches the dataset, significantly mitigating the risk of hallucinations, a common challenge in generative AI applications.

Validation of the system using a controlled scenario demonstrated that the regenerated SOPs achieved similarity scores ranging from 0.8 to 0.9 when compared to the original documents, coming from the manufacturing companies. These results underscore the effectiveness of the RAG framework in reconstructing critical content, structure, and procedural details, despite the absence of direct input data about the hidden SOP. Moreover, the modular design of the pipeline—from data collection and content division to prompt engineering, ensures not only high-quality outputs but also scalability and adaptability to evolving laboratory requirements. The integration of a user-friendly interface, built with the Python Tkinter library, further enables non-technical users to generate customized SOPs seamlessly, thereby bridging the gap between complex technical documentation and practical laboratory needs.

Despite these promising outcomes, several areas remain for further enhancement and exploration. One of the primary challenges is ensuring the continual accuracy and relevance of generated SOPs in a domain characterized by rapid technological and regulatory changes. While the current system effectively minimizes hallucination risks through rigorous data grounding, future iterations could benefit from incorporating real-time data feeds and dynamic updates to reflect the latest regulatory standards and scientific discoveries.

Future work will focus on several key directions:

1.   Enhanced Data Integration and Real-Time Updates: Future research should explore the integration of real-time data sources, such as online regulatory updates, IoT sensor data, and continuously updated scientific databases. This would enable the system to generate SOPs that reflect the most current practices and standards, thereby further reducing the risk of outdated procedures and ensuring compliance with evolving regulations.

2.   Improving Domain Adaptation and Customization: Although the current system is tailored for chemical laboratory workflows, extending the framework to support multiple domains—such as pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, and industrial manufacturing—could significantly broaden its applicability. Future work may involve fine-tuning language models with domain-specific datasets and developing customizable templates that accommodate the unique requirements of various industries.

3.   Advanced Prompt Engineering and Model Optimization: Continued refinement of prompt engineering strategies is essential to enhance the specificity and technical depth of generated SOP sections. Future iterations could incorporate adaptive prompt generation based on user feedback and domain expert evaluations. Additionally, exploring ensemble approaches that combine outputs from multiple models might further reduce the likelihood of hallucinations and improve overall output quality.

4.   User-Centric Enhancements and Usability Studies: The development of the enhanced SOP generator interface marks a significant step toward democratizing the use of advanced AI in technical documentation. Future work should involve conducting extensive user studies and usability testing to gather feedback from laboratory personnel and domain experts. Such studies will be crucial in refining the interface, ensuring that it meets the practical needs of end-users, and identifying any bottlenecks or areas for improvement in the workflow.

5.   Extended Validation and Benchmarking: While the current validation results are promising, additional benchmarking against industry-standard SOPs across a wider range of laboratory scenarios will be necessary. Future research should focus on establishing robust evaluation frameworks that incorporate both quantitative metrics (e.g., similarity scores, retrieval precision) and qualitative assessments (e.g., expert reviews) to comprehensively validate the system’s performance.

6.   Integration with Automated Compliance Monitoring Systems: Finally, integrating the SOP generation platform with automated compliance monitoring and reporting systems could offer substantial benefits. By ensuring that SOPs are not only generated but also continuously monitored for adherence to safety and regulatory standards, organizations can achieve higher levels of operational efficiency and risk management.

This work lays a solid foundation for the automated generation and optimization of SOPs using AI-powered language models and vector database integration. The promising results, coupled with the system’s modular design and user-friendly interface, demonstrate the potential of this approach to revolutionize documentation practices in chemical laboratories. Future research will aim to build upon these advances, addressing current limitations and expanding the system’s capabilities to meet the increasingly complex demands of modern laboratory environments.
